code.title: Dot product and cosine similarity
code.python:
import math

def dot(a, b):
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))  # multiply pairs, add up

def cosine(a, b):
    # divide by both lengths: only direction is left
    return dot(a, b) / (math.sqrt(dot(a, a)) * math.sqrt(dot(b, b)))

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [2, 4, 6]   # same direction as a, twice as long
c = [3, 2, 1]
print("a =", a, "b =", b, "c =", c)
print("dot(a,b) = %d  cosine = %.4f" % (dot(a, b), cosine(a, b)))
print("dot(a,c) = %d  cosine = %.4f" % (dot(a, c), cosine(a, c)))
# normalise once, then a plain dot product equals cosine
na = math.sqrt(dot(a, a)); nc = math.sqrt(dot(c, c))
ua = [x / na for x in a]; uc = [x / nc for x in c]
print("unit dot(a,c) = %.4f" % dot(ua, uc))
# Time O(d) per pair, space O(d)

followUps:
Cosine distance is 1 minus cosine similarity, so it turns a similarity score into a distance where smaller means closer.

Same direction gives 1 − 1 = 0, unrelated vectors give 1, opposite vectors give 2. It is not a true metric, because the triangle inequality can fail, but for ranking nearest neighbours it behaves well. Example: cosine similarity 0.7143 becomes a distance of 0.2857. Many vector databases offer it under names like "cosine" or "angular" distance.

For vectors of length 1, squared Euclidean distance is just a rescaled cosine distance, so both give the same ranking.

Expand the square: |a−b|² = |a|² + |b|² − 2 a·b. With unit vectors that is 1 + 1 − 2cos = 2(1 − cos). Example: cos = 0.5 gives squared distance 1.0, so distance 1. Smaller distance always means larger cosine, which is why normalised embeddings can use any of the three metrics. It fails when vectors are not normalised.

The determinant is the factor by which the matrix scales area (2D) or volume (3D), and a zero determinant means the matrix flattens space and cannot be undone.

[[2,0],[0,1]] has determinant 2: every shape doubles in area. [[0,−1],[1,0]] has determinant 1: a rotation keeps area. [[1,2],[2,4]] has determinant 0: its columns lie on one line, so the whole plane collapses to a line. A negative sign means the orientation is flipped, like a mirror image.

Without a non-linearity, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear layer, so extra depth adds no power.

Two layers compute W2(W1 x) = (W2 W1) x, and W2 W1 is just another matrix. A single matrix can only draw straight boundaries, so it cannot learn something like XOR. Putting ReLU or GELU between the layers bends the space, and then depth lets the network build curved, complex functions. Example: with 2 inputs, no combination of plain linear layers separates XOR, but one hidden layer with ReLU can.

code.title: Matrix multiplication with a shape check
code.python:
def matmul(A, B):
    n, k, k2, m = len(A), len(A[0]), len(B), len(B[0])
    if k != k2:  # inner sizes must match
        return None
    # cell (i, j) = dot product of row i of A and column j of B
    return [[sum(A[i][t] * B[t][j] for t in range(k)) for j in range(m)] for i in range(n)]

A = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]       # 2x3
B = [[7, 8], [9, 10], [11, 12]]  # 3x2
print("A (2x3) @ B (3x2) =", matmul(A, B))   # result is 2x2
print("B (3x2) @ A (2x3) =", matmul(B, A))   # 3x3: order matters
print("A (2x3) @ A (2x3) =", matmul(A, A))   # None: 3 != 2
# Time O(n*k*m), space O(n*m)

followUps:
Multiply from the end that gives the smallest intermediate matrices, because the result is the same but the work is very different.

Take A 10×1000, B 1000×10, C 10×1000. (A·B)·C costs 10·1000·10 + 10·10·1000 = 200,000 multiply-adds. A·(B·C) costs 1000·10·1000 + 10·1000·1000 = 20,000,000. Matrix multiplication is associative, so both are equal. With a vector at the end, always do matrix×vector first. The best order is found with dynamic programming (matrix chain order).

GPUs have thousands of simple cores, and each output cell of a matrix product can be computed independently, so the work spreads out almost perfectly.

A 1,000×1,000 product has a million output cells, each a dot product of 1,000 pairs. The cells need no communication with each other. Matrix multiplication also reuses each loaded number many times, which keeps the cores busy instead of waiting on memory. Modern GPUs have special tensor units that do small blocks of multiply-adds in a single step, often in lower precision such as float16.

The condition number measures how much a small change in the input can be magnified in the answer; a large value means the problem is fragile.

It is the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value, σmax/σmin. A rule of thumb: you lose about log10(κ) digits of accuracy. If κ = 106 and you use float32 (about 7 digits), you keep only about 1 trustworthy digit. Identity has κ = 1 (perfect); a singular matrix has κ = infinity. In NumPy: np.linalg.cond(A).

The pseudo-inverse A⁺ is a generalised inverse that works for any matrix, including non-square or singular ones, and gives the best least-squares answer.

Compute it from the SVD: A = UΣVT gives A⁺ = VΣ⁺UT, where Σ⁺ inverts each non-zero singular value and leaves zeros alone. For an overdetermined system (more equations than unknowns) x = A⁺b minimises |Ax − b|. If several solutions exist, it picks the one with the smallest length. In NumPy: np.linalg.pinv(A) or np.linalg.lstsq.

LU factorisation records the elimination steps as A = L·U (lower times upper triangular), so you can solve for many right-hand sides cheaply.

The expensive elimination, about ⅔n³ operations, is done once. Each new b then costs only two triangular solves, about 2n². Example: n = 1,000 and 100 different b vectors: one factorisation (about 0.67 billion operations) plus 100 × 2 million is far cheaper than redoing elimination 100 times. With pivoting it is P·A = L·U. The same factors also give the determinant.

Run elimination and count the non-zero rows left in the triangular form; that count is the rank.

Example: rows [1,2,3], [2,4,6], [1,0,1]. Subtract 2×row 1 from row 2 and row 1 from row 3: [0,0,0] and [0,−2,−2]. Two non-zero rows remain, so rank 2. A row of zeros means a dependent row. In floating point, treat tiny values as zero using a tolerance, which is why libraries use SVD for rank: np.linalg.matrix_rank(A).

code.title: Power iteration finds the dominant eigenvector
code.python:
import math

M = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]  # eigenvalues 3 and 1; dominant direction [1, 1]
v = [1.0, 0.0]        # arbitrary start with some part along the top direction

def mul(M, v):
    return [sum(M[i][j] * v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(M))]

for step in range(20):
    w = mul(M, v)                           # apply the matrix
    norm = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in w))
    v = [x / norm for x in w]               # rescale to length 1

Mv = mul(M, v)
lam = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(v, Mv)) / sum(a * a for a in v)  # Rayleigh quotient
print("matrix =", M)
print("eigenvalue = %.4f" % lam)
print("eigenvector = [%.4f, %.4f]" % (v[0], v[1]))
# Time O(steps * n^2) dense, space O(n)

followUps:
Find the dominant eigenvector first, then remove its contribution (deflation) and run power iteration again.

For a symmetric matrix A with top pair (λ1, v1), form A' = A − λ1·v1·v1T. Now λ1 is replaced by 0, so the largest remaining value is λ2. Example: for [[2,1],[1,2]], λ1 = 3 and v1 = [1,1]/√2; A' = [[0.5,−0.5],[−0.5,0.5]], whose top eigenvector is [1,−1]/√2 with value 1. Rounding errors build up, so for many components use a proper eigen-solver instead.

A covariance matrix is a sum of squares, and a sum of squares cannot be negative, so its eigenvalues cannot be negative.

For centred data X, C = XTX/(n−1). For any direction v, vTCv = |Xv|²/(n−1) ≥ 0, and for an eigenvector this equals λ. That value is the variance of the data along v, and variance is never negative. Example: if a feature is constant, the eigenvalue is exactly 0. A tiny negative value like −1e−17 is rounding noise.

Without centring, the first component mostly points at the data's average position instead of the direction of greatest spread.

Example: points near (100, 100) with small variation. Uncentred, the top direction is about [1,1]/√2 because all points are far from the origin, even if the spread is entirely sideways. The explained variance numbers also become wrong, because they include the mean. Always subtract the per-feature mean, using the mean from the training set. Libraries such as scikit-learn do the centring for you, but a hand-written version does not.

PCA hurts when the useful signal lives in low-variance directions, or when the relationship is non-linear.

Examples: a feature that predicts the label but has tiny variance gets dropped, while a noisy high-variance feature is kept. Unscaled features let the one with big units dominate (salary in dollars against age). Data on a curve or spiral is not captured by straight directions. It also makes features hard to explain. Check the accuracy of the downstream model with and without PCA.

Randomised SVD finds a small subspace that captures most of the matrix using random projections, then does an exact SVD on a much smaller matrix.

Steps: multiply A (m×n) by a random n×(k+p) matrix, orthonormalise the result with QR to get Q, then take the SVD of the small matrix QTA. Cost is about O(m·n·k) instead of O(m·n·min(m,n)). For a 1,000,000×10,000 matrix and k = 50 this is a big saving. The answer is approximate but usually very close for the top singular values. scikit-learn uses it for large PCA.

Forming XTX squares the condition number, so small singular values get lost in rounding error, while SVD works on X directly.

Example: if σmax = 104 and σmin = 10−4, then κ = 108, but XTX has κ = 1016, which float64 (about 16 digits) cannot represent. The small component becomes noise. SVD avoids that step and is also the stable path to least squares. XTX is cheaper to form when columns are few and well-behaved.

The dot products grow with the number of dimensions, and dividing by √dk keeps their spread near 1 so softmax does not saturate.

If each entry of q and k has mean 0 and variance 1, the dot product of dk terms has variance dk, so its typical size is √dk. For dk = 64 raw scores are around ±8, and softmax becomes almost one-hot with tiny gradients. Dividing by 8 brings the variance back to 1.

The KV cache stores the key and value vectors of every token already processed, so generating the next token does not recompute them.

Each new token needs only its own query, which attends over the cached K and V. Per layer, per token, the cache holds 2 × (heads × dk) numbers. Example: 32 layers, 4,096 width, float16, 2,000 tokens: 2 × 4,096 × 2 bytes × 32 × 2,000 is about 1 GB. Memory grows linearly with context length, which is why it limits batch size.

HNSW builds a layered graph of nearby vectors and finds neighbours by walking greedily downhill towards the query.

Each vector is linked to a few close neighbours. The top layers are sparse, with long links that act as highways; the bottom layer holds everyone. A search enters at the top, moves to the neighbour closest to the query until none is closer, drops a layer, and repeats. The cost is roughly logarithmic in the number of vectors. Key settings: M (links per node) and efSearch (candidates kept), which trade recall against speed and memory.

Treat the index in two parts: apply writes to a small fresh index at once, and rebuild or merge in the background.

HNSW supports adding new points online, but deletes are awkward, so they are usually marked as tombstones, filtered from results, and cleaned during a periodic rebuild. IVF needs retraining if the data drifts. A common design: a large read-only index plus a small live one, with queries merged across both. Example: add 100k vectors a day to 10M, rebuild weekly, and monitor recall on a fixed test set.

Cholesky factorisation writes a symmetric positive-definite matrix as A = L·LT with L lower triangular, and it is used to solve systems and to sample correlated random numbers.

It takes about ⅓n³ operations, half of LU. Uses: solving A x = b in Gaussian processes and ridge regression; testing whether a matrix is positive definite (it fails if not); and sampling from a multivariate normal as x = μ + L·z with z standard normal. Example: A = [[4,2],[2,3]] gives L = [[2,0],[1,√2]].

A negative Hessian eigenvalue means the loss curves downward along that direction, so the point is a saddle or a maximum there, not a minimum.

At a true minimum all eigenvalues are ≥ 0. Example: the loss x² − y² has Hessian eigenvalues +2 and −2, so moving along y lowers the loss. In high-dimensional networks, saddle points are far more common than bad local minima, and noise from SGD and momentum helps escape them. Second-order methods use this information, and a mix of signs indicates a saddle.

The test that the rows of the attention weights sum to 1 catches a wrong softmax axis.

If softmax runs over the wrong axis, the columns sum to 1 instead, and the row sums become arbitrary. Check weights.sum(axis=-1) equals ones within a tolerance. Use a non-square or asymmetric case, because with a symmetric score matrix both axes happen to give the same sums. A causal-mask check also helps: token i must put zero weight on tokens after i.

Test properties that hold for both signs instead of comparing the vectors directly.

An eigenvector v and −v are equally valid. So check A v ≈ λ v, check the vector has length 1, or compare up to sign with abs(dot(v, expected)) ≈ 1. Eigenvalues are unique, so compare those directly. Example: assert abs(abs(v @ ref) - 1) < 1e-9. For repeated eigenvalues, compare the subspace instead (projection matrices), because any rotation inside it is valid.
